name: Panchase
tagline: Forest summit at 2,517 m where Kaski, Parbat and Syangja meet
meta_description: Panchase guide: the 2,517 m summit west of Pokhara, sunrise over Dhaulagiri and Annapurna, sacred ponds, orchid forest, lodges at Bhanjyang and trek options.
summary: Panchase is a forested hill at about 2,517 m west of Phewa Lake, the highest point in the Pokhara area. A 1–1.5 hour climb from the lodges at Panchase Bhanjyang leads to a summit view from Dhaulagiri to Manaslu, with Phewa Lake below. It is quieter than Sarangkot or Australian Camp and rich in orchids and birds.
intro: Panchase rises where three districts meet, Kaski, Parbat and Syangja, about 20 km west of Pokhara in a straight line. Its upper slopes are covered in dense forest of oak, rhododendron and laurel, protected since the early 2010s as the Panchase Protected Forest. The name means five lakes, after a group of small sacred ponds near the summit, and a shrine there draws Hindu pilgrims as well as trekkers. It is the highest point in the area.

The summit view is the widest in the Pokhara area. On clear mornings you see Dhaulagiri and the Dhaulagiri range to the north-west, the full Annapurna massif, Machhapuchhre straight ahead, Lamjung Himal and Manaslu to the east, and in the opposite direction the hills of Syangja rolling south towards the plains. Phewa Lake shines in the valley to the east, with Pokhara beyond it. Few other viewpoints near Pokhara show both Dhaulagiri and Manaslu at once.

Most visitors reach Panchase on a two- to three-day trek from Pokhara, crossing Phewa by boat and climbing through villages such as Bhumdi and Pumdikot, or drive to Panchase Bhanjyang, the saddle below the summit where simple lodges stand. Few foreign trekkers come, so the trails are quiet, and the forest's orchids, over a hundred species by local counts, make it popular with naturalists in spring and summer. Lodges are simple, which keeps the crowds away.

≈ 2–3 h by jeep to Bhanjyang, or 2 days' walk
Highest viewpoint near Pokhara, sacred ponds, orchid forest

highlights.title: Summit panorama
highlights.text: From the top at about 2,517 m, the skyline runs from Dhaulagiri past the Annapurnas and Machhapuchhre to Manaslu. It is the broadest Himalayan view within a day of Pokhara, and on most mornings you share it with only a handful of people.

highlights.title: Sacred ponds and shrine
highlights.text: Near the summit a small temple stands beside a group of ponds that give Panchase its name. Pilgrims ring bells, light incense and tie prayer flags. Local fairs bring crowds on certain full-moon days. Visitors of all faiths are welcome.

highlights.title: Orchid and rhododendron forest
highlights.text: The protected forest holds a large number of orchid species, many flowering between April and August, plus rhododendron, magnolia and oak. It is one of the richest forest walks near Pokhara for plants and birds.

highlights.title: Phewa Lake from above
highlights.text: On the walk up from Bhumdi and on the eastern side of the summit, Phewa Lake lies far below with the World Peace Pagoda and Lakeside visible. Few viewpoints show the whole lake and the mountains together so well.

highlights.title: Quiet village trails
highlights.text: Trails to Panchase pass Gurung, Magar and Brahmin villages such as Bhumdi, Thulakharka and Bhadaure, with terraced fields and small tea shops. It feels far more remote than the distance from Pokhara suggests. Tea shops serve walkers along the way.

how_to_reach.text: Jeep roads now reach Panchase Bhanjyang from the Pokhara side and from Syangja, about 2–3 hours from Pokhara by four-wheel drive depending on the route and road condition. Roads can be rough and are often blocked by landslides in the monsoon, so check current status before you travel.

The classic trek crosses Phewa Lake by boat to Pame or starts at Damside, climbs via Bhumdi and Thulakharka to Panchase Bhanjyang in about 2 days of 5–6 hours each, then climbs 1–1.5 hours to the summit for sunrise. Return via Bhadaure and Naudanda to the Baglung road, or down to Phewa's west end.

where_to_stay: Panchase Bhanjyang, the saddle at about 2,050 m below the summit, has a few simple trekking lodges and teahouses with twin rooms, shared bathrooms and dal bhat kitchens. Villages along the trek routes, such as Bhumdi, Thulakharka and Bhadaure, offer basic lodges and community homestays. Facilities are simpler than on the main Annapurna trails, hot water is limited and it is cold at night from December to February. In Pokhara, before and after the trek, our guests stay at Lakeside hotels such as Hotel Barahi or Temple Tree Resort & Spa.
tips: Leave Panchase Bhanjyang about 75 minutes before sunrise for the summit; the trail is steep but short.
Bring a warm jacket, hat and gloves, as the summit at 2,517 m is close to freezing at dawn in winter.
Carry enough Nepali cash for the whole trek, as there are no ATMs and few lodges accept cards.
Use a local guide: trails through the forest have many unmarked junctions.
Avoid June to August, when the forest trails are muddy and leeches are common.

experiences.title: Panchase summit sunrise hike
experiences.summary: A pre-dawn climb of about 450 m from Panchase Bhanjyang through dark forest to the summit at about 2,517 m, timed for first light on Dhaulagiri, the Annapurnas, Machhapuchhre and Manaslu. The highest and widest sunrise viewpoint in the Pokhara area.
body: Set off from your lodge at Panchase Bhanjyang with head torches about 75 minutes before sunrise. The trail climbs steeply through oak and rhododendron forest on earth and stone steps, gaining roughly 450 m. Most walkers take 1–1.5 hours. Near the top the trees thin and you pass the shrine and ponds before reaching the open summit area with a viewing platform. Walk at a steady pace and stop to catch your breath rather than rushing; there is time.

As the sky brightens, the Himalaya appears from end to end: Dhaulagiri and its neighbours in the north-west, the Annapurna massif with Annapurna South and Hiunchuli in front, Machhapuchhre, Annapurna II, Lamjung Himal and Manaslu far to the east. To the south and west lie ridges of Syangja and Parbat, and to the east, Phewa Lake catches the first light below. It is one of the few places near Pokhara where Dhaulagiri and Manaslu are both in view.

Stay 30–45 minutes, then descend to Bhanjyang for breakfast, about an hour. Clear sunrises are most likely from October to December. March and April bring rhododendron flowers along the trail but more haze. Bring warm layers, gloves and a thermos of tea; it is close to freezing at dawn from December to February. A local guide is strongly recommended for the forest junctions in the dark. Breakfast at the lodge tastes very good after the climb.

faqs.q: How hard is the Panchase summit hike?
faqs.a: Moderate. From Panchase Bhanjyang at about 2,050 m it is a steep climb of roughly 450 m to the summit at 2,517 m, taking 1–1.5 hours up and about an hour down. Reasonable fitness and good shoes are needed. Altitude is not a problem for healthy walkers at this height.

faqs.q: What can you see from Panchase?
faqs.a: On clear mornings: Dhaulagiri, the Annapurna range, Machhapuchhre, Lamjung Himal and Manaslu across the north, Phewa Lake and Pokhara to the east, and the hills of Syangja and Parbat to the south and west. It is the widest panorama in the Pokhara area.

faqs.q: Is Panchase better than Sarangkot for sunrise?
faqs.a: Panchase is about 900 m higher and shows more of the range, including Manaslu, with almost no crowds. Sarangkot is reachable by car in 40 minutes and is far easier. Choose Panchase if you are happy with a trek or a long jeep ride and a basic lodge night.

experiences.title: Panchase sacred ponds and hilltop shrine
experiences.best_time: Morning; local fairs on some full-moon days
experiences.summary: Near the summit of Panchase, a small temple and a group of ponds draw Hindu pilgrims from Kaski, Parbat and Syangja. Visit after sunrise to see local devotees ring bells and light incense among the prayer flags and forest.
body: Panchase takes its name from five small lakes, more accurately ponds, on the upper slopes of the hill. A simple temple stands beside them, decorated with bells, tridents and prayer flags, and is one of the most important hill shrines in this part of the Middle Hills. Shepherds, farmers and pilgrims from the surrounding districts come to pray for rain, good harvests and the health of their animals. Prayer flags hang between the trees around the ponds.

On ordinary days the shrine is quiet, with perhaps a few local visitors and the sound of wind in the trees. On certain full-moon days and festivals, local fairs bring hundreds of pilgrims who climb from villages on all sides, bathe in or sprinkle themselves with pond water and make offerings. Festival dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current dates before you travel if you want to see one.

Treat the area with respect: walk clockwise around the shrine, do not wash or throw anything into the ponds, and ask before photographing people at prayer. The shrine is a few minutes below the summit viewpoint, so pilgrims and trekkers combine both on the sunrise climb from Panchase Bhanjyang. Pilgrims usually visit after sunrise, when the summit crowd has dispersed and the shrine is quiet again. Keep the area clean and carry all litter back down to the lodges at Bhanjyang, as there are no bins on the summit.

faqs.a: The ponds near the summit, which give Panchase its name meaning five lakes, are considered holy, and a shrine beside them is worshipped by Hindu communities in Kaski, Parbat and Syangja. Pilgrims come to pray for rain, health and good harvests, and local fairs are held on certain full-moon days.

faqs.q: Can non-Hindus visit the Panchase shrine?
faqs.a: Yes. The shrine is open-air and visitors of all faiths are welcome to look and walk around respectfully. Remove shoes if asked, walk clockwise and avoid touching offerings or the ponds. Ask before photographing worshippers, especially during fairs. Donations are welcome.

Local fairs are held at the shrine on certain full-moon days and religious festivals, which follow the lunar calendar and move each year. They can be crowded and lively. Ask your guide or check current dates before you travel if you want to attend or to avoid the crowds.

experiences.title: Orchid and bird walk in Panchase forest
experiences.best_time: Apr–Jun for orchids; Oct–Dec for clear views
experiences.summary: A slow walk with a naturalist through the Panchase Protected Forest, one of the best places near Pokhara for wild orchids, rhododendrons, magnolias and Himalayan forest birds. Spring brings flowers; autumn brings views. Go slowly to see more.
body: The upper slopes of Panchase between about 1,800 and 2,500 m are cloaked in moist broadleaf forest of oak, laurel, rhododendron and magnolia, kept damp by monsoon cloud and protected from felling since the early 2010s. Moss and ferns cover the trunks, and many of the trees host epiphytic orchids. Local conservation groups report well over a hundred orchid species here, which makes Panchase a draw for botanists. Many grow high on trunks and branches.

With a naturalist guide, walk the forest trails around Panchase Bhanjyang and the summit ridge. From late March to May, rhododendrons flower red and pink and the first orchids appear; the main orchid season continues into the monsoon months of June to August, though rain and leeches make walking harder then. Look also for birds such as laughingthrushes, yuhinas, sunbirds, flycatchers and woodpeckers, and listen for barking deer. Wet-season walking can be rewarding with care.

Do not pick or collect orchids; it is illegal and the forest relies on visitors to protect it. Wear long trousers and closed shoes, carry a rain jacket and bring binoculars and a macro lens or phone for flowers. Combine the walk with the summit sunrise for a full day at Panchase. A naturalist guide makes a big difference here, pointing out small flowers you would otherwise walk past and identifying birds by call. Allow 3–4 hours, and expect mist on the ridge even on fine mornings.

faqs.q: When do orchids flower at Panchase?
faqs.a: Different species flower from spring through the monsoon, with the most flowers from about April to August. Rhododendrons bloom from late March to May. The monsoon months bring the most orchids but also rain, mud and leeches. April and May are a good compromise for flowers and walking conditions.

Yes. Panchase's upper forest was declared a protected forest in the early 2010s, managed with local community forest user groups to conserve its orchids, plants and wildlife. Collecting plants is prohibited. No national park permit is required as of our last check, but check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What wildlife lives in Panchase forest?
faqs.a: Common sightings are forest birds such as laughingthrushes, sunbirds, barbets and woodpeckers, plus langur and rhesus monkeys. Barking deer and leopard live in the forest but are rarely seen. Spring mornings are best for birds. Walk quietly with a local guide to see more.

Panchase is a forested hill about 20 km west of Pokhara in a straight line, where the districts of Kaski, Parbat and Syangja meet. Its summit at about 2,517 m is the highest point near Pokhara. Panchase Bhanjyang, the saddle with lodges below the summit, is about 2–3 hours by jeep from Pokhara.

faqs.q: How many days is the Panchase trek?
faqs.a: Usually 2–3 days from Pokhara. A common plan crosses Phewa Lake by boat, walks via Bhumdi to Panchase Bhanjyang over two days, climbs to the summit for sunrise on day three and descends via Bhadaure to the Baglung road. By jeep to Bhanjyang, it can be done in one night.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Panchase?
faqs.a: Panchase lies outside the Annapurna Conservation Area and is a protected forest, so as of our last check no ACAP or national park permit is required, though local fees may be charged. Rules for foreign trekkers and guides change, so check current status before you travel.

It is easy to moderate. Walking days are 5–6 hours on village and forest trails with some steep sections, and the highest point is about 2,517 m, too low for serious altitude problems. Facilities are basic. Families with active teenagers and fit seniors can manage it with a guide.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Panchase?
faqs.a: October to December for clear mountain views and dry trails. March to May for rhododendrons and early orchids, with more haze. June to August brings orchids but heavy rain, mud and leeches. January and February are clear but cold at night.

Yes, a few simple trekking lodges and teahouses at Panchase Bhanjyang and basic lodges or homestays in villages such as Bhumdi, Thulakharka and Bhadaure. Expect twin rooms, shared bathrooms and dal bhat meals. Facilities are more basic than on the main Annapurna trails.

faqs.q: Can I combine Panchase with the World Peace Pagoda?
faqs.a: Yes. The classic trek starts with a boat across Phewa to the south shore, a climb to the World Peace Pagoda and onward along the ridge via Bhumdi towards Panchase. This turns the first half-day of the trek into a sightseeing walk with views back over Phewa and Pokhara.

faqs.q: Is Panchase suitable for a short trek with kids?
faqs.a: Yes for active older children. The jeep option to Panchase Bhanjyang with one night and a summit sunrise is manageable for children from about ten. The full walking trek suits teenagers who are used to hiking. Bring warm clothes for cold nights and mornings.

faqs.q: Panchase or Australian Camp: which should I choose?
faqs.a: Australian Camp is easier, closer to Machhapuchhre and has better lodges, with a 1–1.5 hour walk from the road. Panchase is higher, quieter and has a wider view including Dhaulagiri and Manaslu, but needs a longer jeep ride or trek and simpler lodges. First-timers usually choose Australian Camp.
